summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in output feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option, defining two key sizes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2949 specifies how Telnet can encrypt data with CAST-128 in output feedback mode. It also warns that this mode does not detect tampering and that the 40-bit key variant is not secure.

questions: how does telnet cast-128 ofb64 work
does telnet ofb64 protect data integrity
subtitle: How Telnet uses CAST-128 in 64-bit output feedback mode.

tldr.problem: Telnet's encryption option needs a defined way to use CAST-128 in output feedback mode with negotiated keys.
tldr.mechanism: The encrypting side sends an 8-byte initial vector, negotiates a key identifier, and then encrypts data using CAST-128 OFB64.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines 40-bit and 128-bit key variants, while warning that output feedback does not ensure data integrity and 40-bit keys are not secure.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 2949's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC defines Telnet use of CAST-128 output feedback and documents limitations of the mode.

sections.title: Setting Up CAST-128 OFB64
sections.content:
The RFC defines CAST-128 in output feedback mode for Telnet's encryption option, with 40-bit and 128-bit key variants. The side that will encrypt generates a random 8-byte initial vector and sends it in clear text to the other side.

After the receiver accepts the vector, the sides negotiate a key identifier. Once they have a common key identifier, the encrypting side can send START and END commands to control encryption. A changed key identifier or initial vector requires the encryption state to be reinitialized.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers exchange an initial vector and agree on a key identifier before encrypting Telnet data. The vector is sent openly, while it helps set the encryption state.

sections.title: How Output Feedback Processes Data
sections.content:
The algorithm begins by applying CAST to the initial vector with the key. It repeatedly transforms the prior state and combines that result with each 64-bit block of input to produce output.

The RFC also describes how the default key may come from the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option. If there is insufficient key material for a given variant, that encryption option must not be offered or used.
sections.plainLanguage: The method creates a stream of output from the key and initial vector, then combines it with the data. Both sides need matching key material and state to encrypt and decrypt correctly.

sections.title: Integrity and Key-Size Warnings
sections.content:
The RFC states that output feedback encryption does not ensure data integrity. An active attacker may be able to substitute text when the clear text can be predicted.

The document says the 40-bit-key mode is not to be considered secure and is included to document existing implementations. It also questions whether output feedback should be deprecated in favor of cipher feedback modes, given its weaknesses.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption can hide data without proving that nobody changed it. The RFC explicitly says the 40-bit version is not secure.
